<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Let $j,x\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $y,z$ be distinct positive integers.
The $(j,x,y,z)$-hiccup sequence has $a(1)=x$ and, for $n\geq2$,
\begin{equation}
 a(n)=a(n-1)+
 \begin{cases}
 y,&n-j\in\{a(1),\ldots,a(n-1)\},\\
 z,&n-j\notin\{a(1),\ldots,a(n-1)\}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The first case is a \emph{hit} and the second a \emph{miss}.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:complement}
For every integer $q\geq1$, the $(0,q+2,1,2)$-hiccup sequence $a_q$
has an infinite complement. For $n,j\geq1$,
\begin{align}
 a_q(n)&=n+q+C_q(n),\label{eq:aC}\\
 c_q(j+q)&=c_q(j)+j+q-1,\label{eq:comprec}\\
 c_q(j+1)-c_q(j)&=\left\lceil j/q\right\rceil.\label{eq:gaps}
\end{align}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Since every increment is positive and $a_q(n)\geq n+q+1$, an integer
$n$ that occurs as a value occurs before step $n$. For $n\geq2$, step
$n$ is therefore a miss exactly when $n$ lies in the complement, which
begins with $1,2,\ldots,q+1$. Summing the increments gives
\[
 a_q(n)=q+2+(n-1)+(C_q(n)-1),
\]
and this is~\eqref{eq:aC}, also for $n=1$.

At a missing index $c_q(j)\geq2$ the sequence jumps by $2$ and skips
the single integer
\[
 a_q(c_q(j))-1=c_q(j)+q+j-1.
\]
Every missing integer larger than $q+1$ is skipped in this way, and the
skipped integers increase with $j$. The complement is infinite, since
if it were finite, its largest element would produce a larger one. The
integer skipped at $c_q(j)$ is preceded in the complement by the $q+1$
initial missing integers and by the $j-2$ integers skipped at
$c_q(2),\ldots,c_q(j-1)$, so its rank is $j+q$. This
is~\eqref{eq:comprec} for $j\geq2$, and for $j=1$ the identity reduces
to $c_q(q+1)=q+1$.

The differences $d_j=c_q(j+1)-c_q(j)$ satisfy $d_{j+q}=d_j+1$
by~\eqref{eq:comprec}, and $d_1=\cdots=d_q=1$,
so~\eqref{eq:gaps} follows.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:allclosed}
For $q,n\geq1$, let
\[
 M=\left\lfloor \frac{q+\sqrt{q^2+8q(n-1)}}{2q}\right\rfloor.
\]
Then
\begin{align}
 C_q(n)&=q(M-1)+1+\left\lfloor \frac{n-B_q(M)}M\right\rfloor,\\
 a_q(n)&=n+qM+1+\left\lfloor \frac{n-B_q(M)}M\right\rfloor.
\end{align}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The choice of $M$ means that $B_q(M)\leq n<B_q(M+1)$. There are
$q(M-1)$ missing integers below $B_q(M)$ and
$1+\lfloor(n-B_q(M))/M\rfloor$ in $[B_q(M),n]$. This gives the
formula for $C_q(n)$. The formula for $a_q(n)$ follows
from~\eqref{eq:aC}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:radical}
For $1\leq q\leq7$ and $n\geq1$,
\begin{align}
 C_q(n)
 &=\left\lceil \sqrt{2qn}-\frac q2\right\rceil
 =\left\lfloor \frac{2-q+\sqrt{q^2+8q(n-1)}}2\right\rfloor,\label{eq:radical}\\
 a_q(n)&=\left\lceil \bigl(\sqrt n+\sqrt{q/2}\bigr)^2\right\rceil.
 \label{eq:hiccupradical}
\end{align}
For every $q\geq8$, each expression in~\eqref{eq:radical} fails for
some $n$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Put
\[
 \tau_q(j)=1+\frac{(j-1)(j+q-1)}{2q},\qquad
 y_q(j)=\frac{(2j-2+q)^2}{8q}.
\]
Writing $j-1=qm+r$, with $0\leq r<q$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:roundingerror}
 c_q(j)-\tau_q(j)=\frac{r(q-r)}{2q},\qquad
 y_q(j)+1-c_q(j)=\frac{(q-2r)^2}{8q}.
\end{equation}
The floor expression in~\eqref{eq:radical} first reaches the value $j$
at $n=\lceil\tau_q(j)\rceil$, and this equals $c_q(j)$ for all $j$ if
and only if $r(q-r)<2q$ for every residue $r$. As
$\max_r r(q-r)=\lfloor q^2/4\rfloor$, this means $q\leq7$.

For these $q$ the number $\sqrt{2qn}-q/2$ is positive, and its ceiling
is at least $j$ if and only if $n>y_q(j)$. The second identity
in~\eqref{eq:roundingerror} shows that
\[
0\leq y_q(j)+1-c_q(j)\leq q/8<1,
\]
so $\lfloor y_q(j)\rfloor+1=c_q(j)$. Thus the ceiling expression and
$C_q(n)$ are both at least $j$ exactly when $n\geq c_q(j)$. Then~\eqref{eq:aC}
yields~\eqref{eq:hiccupradical}. For $q\geq8$ the ceiling expression
is at most $0$ at $n=1$, whereas $C_q(1)=1$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:q8}
For every $n\geq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q8}
 a_8(n)=\left\lceil (\sqrt n+2)^2\right\rceil
       +\mathbf1_{\{n\text{ is an odd square}\}}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For $q=8$ the second quantity in~\eqref{eq:roundingerror} is at most
$1$, with equality if and only if $r=0$. Hence the ceiling expression
reaches the value $j$ at $c_8(j)$ when $r\neq0$, and at $c_8(j)+1$
when $r=0$. Since $c_8(8m+1)=1+4m(m+1)=(2m+1)^2$, the ceiling
expression is smaller than $C_8$ by $1$ exactly at the odd squares.
Adding $n+8$ gives~\eqref{eq:q8}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
For $q,n\geq1$, define $\theta_q(n)$ by
\[
a_q(n)=n+\sqrt{2qn}+\frac q2+\theta_q(n).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
0\leq\theta_q(n)
\leq1+\sqrt{2qn+\frac{q(q-8)}4}-\sqrt{2qn}
\leq1+\frac{\max\{0,q(q-8)\}}{8\sqrt{2qn}}.
\end{equation}
For $q\leq7$ this gives $0\leq\theta_q(n)<1$. For $q=8$, both endpoints
of $0\leq\theta_8(n)\leq1$ are attained infinitely often.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $j=C_q(n)$, so that $\theta_q(n)=j+q/2-\sqrt{2qn}$
by~\eqref{eq:aC}. By~\eqref{eq:roundingerror},
$\tau_q(j)\leq c_q(j)\leq\tau_q(j)+q/8$. Combined with
$n\leq c_q(j+1)-1$, this gives
\[
n\leq\tau_q(j+1)+\frac q8-1
 =\frac{(j+q/2)^2}{2q},
\]
that is, $j+q/2\geq\sqrt{2qn}$, which is the lower bound. In the other
direction, $\tau_q(j)\leq c_q(j)\leq n$ implies
\[
j+\frac q2\leq1+\sqrt{2qn+\frac{q(q-8)}4},
\]
which is the middle bound. For $q<8$ the difference of square roots is
negative, so $\theta_q(n)<1$, and for $q\geq8$ rationalizing it yields
the last bound. Finally, Corollary~\ref{cor:q8} shows that $\theta_8$
equals $0$ at the even squares and $1$ at the odd squares.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
For every integer $q\geq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:theta}
H_q(z)=\frac z2\sum_{r=0}^{q-1}f(z^r,z^{q-r})
       -\frac{(q-1)z}{2},
\end{equation}
as formal power series in $z$, each theta function being expanded in
powers of $z$, and hence for $|z|<1$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For $0\leq r<q$ put
\[
S_r(z)=\sum_{\nu\geq1}z^{q\nu(\nu-1)/2+r\nu}.
\]
The substitution $\nu=m+1$ in~\eqref{eq:missingGF} gives
$H_q(z)=z\sum_{r=0}^{q-1}S_r(z)$. On the other hand
$S_0(z)=\psi(z^q)=\tfrac12f(1,z^q)$, and for $1\leq r<q$ the terms of
index $\nu\geq1$, $\nu=0$, and $\nu\leq-1$ of the bilateral series give
\[
f(z^r,z^{q-r})=S_r(z)+1+S_{q-r}(z).
\]
Summing over $r$ yields~\eqref{eq:theta}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:nested}
For $q\geq1$, the function $C_q$ is the unique sequence with $C_q(n)=n$ for
$1\leq n\leq q$ and
\begin{equation}
 C_q(n)=q+C_q\bigl(n-C_q(n-1)\bigr)\qquad(n>q),
\end{equation}
where both arguments on the right lie in $\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Exactly $r$ values of $a_q$ are at most $a_q(r)$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:invariant}
 C_q(a_q(r))=a_q(r)-r=q+C_q(r).
\end{equation}
For $n>q$, the number $r=n-C_q(n-1)$ is $1$ plus the number of
values of $a_q$ below $n$, so $a_q(r)$ is the first value that is at
least $n$. Since $a_q(1)=q+2\leq n+1$ and later steps add at most $2$,
either $a_q(r)=n$, or $a_q(r)=n+1$ and $n$ is missing. In both cases
$C_q(n)=C_q(a_q(r))$, and the recurrence follows from~\eqref{eq:invariant}.
Since $1\leq C_q(n-1)\leq n-1$, both arguments lie in $\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$,
and uniqueness follows by induction.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:generalnested}
Let $x\geq2$ and $k\geq1$ be integers. Let $g$ be the
$(0,x,1,k+1)$-hiccup sequence, and let
$U(n)$ count the positive integers at most $n$ outside $\operatorname{im}(g)$, with
$U(0)=0$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:generaltransform}
 g(n)=n+x-k-1+kU(n).
\end{equation}
For $n\geq\max\{2,k,x-1\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:generalnested}
 U(n)=x-k-1+
 \sum_{i=1}^{k}U\bigl(n-i+1-U(n-i)\bigr),
\end{equation}
and every argument on the right is a positive integer smaller than $n$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Since $g(n)>n$, step $n\geq2$ is a hit if and only if $n\in\operatorname{im}(g)$. As
$1\notin\operatorname{im}(g)$, steps $2$ to $n$ contain $U(n)-1$ misses, and summing
the increments gives~\eqref{eq:generaltransform}.

For $t\geq1$ put $F(t)=U(t-U(t-1))$. As in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:nested}, $t-U(t-1)$ is the index of the first value
of $g$ that is at least $t$. Hence $F(1)=1$, and $F$ increases by $1$
exactly at the integers
\[
 \delta_j=g(j-1)+1\qquad(j\geq2,\ j\notin\operatorname{im}(g)).
\]
The miss at step $j$ skips the $k$ integers
$\delta_j,\delta_j+1,\ldots,\delta_j+k-1$, and these pairwise disjoint
blocks, together with $1,\ldots,x-1$, make up the complement. For
$n\geq\max\{k,x-1\}$ we therefore have
\begin{align*}
 U(n)&=x-1+\sum_j\min\{k,\max\{0,n-\delta_j+1\}\},\\
 \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}F(n-i)
     &=k+\sum_j\min\{k,\max\{0,n-\delta_j+1\}\},
\end{align*}
where only finitely many summands are nonzero. Subtracting gives
\eqref{eq:generalnested}. If $n-i\geq1$, then
$1\leq U(n-i)\leq n-i$ and the argument $n-i+1-U(n-i)$ lies in
$[1,n-i]$. Otherwise $n=i=k$, and the argument is $1-U(0)=1<n$ because
$n\geq2$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:tree}
Let $x\geq2$ and $k\geq1$ be integers, and let $K_h$ be the complete ordered
$k$-ary tree of height $h$, with $K_0$ a single leaf. Let $T_{-1}$ be a
single leaf and, for $h\geq0$, form $T_h$ by attaching to a new root,
in order, the tree $T_{h-1}$ followed by $x-2$ copies of $K_h$. Label
each $T_h$ in postorder, starting at $1$.

For every integer $n\geq1$, choose $h$ with $|T_h|\geq n$. The leaf
labels at most $n$ are exactly the positive integers at most $n$
missing from the $(0,x,1,k+1)$-hiccup sequence. Their number
is therefore $U(n)$, independently of the choice of $h$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Encode leaves by $0$ and internal vertices by $1$. The postorder word
$W_h$ of $K_h$ satisfies $W_0=0$ and $W_{h+1}=W_h^k1$, so
$W_h=\phi^h(0)$ for the morphism $\phi(0)=0^k1$, $\phi(1)=1$. Since
$T_{h-1}$ is the first subtree of $T_h$, its vertices keep their labels
and their leaf status in $T_h$, and the postorder words of
$T_0,T_1,\ldots$ are successive prefixes of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:treeword}
 0\prod_{h\geq0}\bigl(W_h^{\,x-2}1\bigr).
\end{equation}
By the result of Fokkink and Joshi~\cite[Lemma 5, Equation (6)]{FJ},
the characteristic word of the $(0,x,1,k+1)$-hiccup sequence is
obtained from the fixed point of
\[
 \beta\longmapsto\beta0^{x-2}1,\qquad
 0\longmapsto0^k1,\qquad1\longmapsto1
\]
starting with $\beta$ by replacing $\beta$ with $0$. The
blocks appended at successive iterations are
$\phi^h(0^{x-2}1)=W_h^{\,x-2}1$, so this word is~\eqref{eq:treeword},
and its zeros are the missing integers.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:iterates}
For integers $q,n\geq1$ and $t\geq0$,
\begin{align}
 C_q\bigl(a_q^{\circ t}(n)\bigr)&=C_q(n)+qt,\label{eq:itercount}\\
 a_q^{\circ t}(n)&=n+tC_q(n)+q\binom{t+1}{2}.\label{eq:iterate}
\end{align}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 a_q^{\circ t}(1)=P_q(t),\qquad
 \mathcal T(\widehat P_q)=P_q.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Iterating~\eqref{eq:invariant} yields~\eqref{eq:itercount}.
By~\eqref{eq:aC}, the step from $a_q^{\circ h}(n)$ to
$a_q^{\circ(h+1)}(n)$ is $q+C_q(n)+qh$, and summing over $0\leq h<t$
gives~\eqref{eq:iterate}. With $n=1$ and $C_q(1)=1$ this is $P_q(t)$,
and by~\eqref{eq:KBidentification} the orbit of $1$ under
$a_q=\widehat P_q^{\,*}$ is $\mathcal T(\widehat P_q)$ by definition.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:fC}
For every $q,n\geq1$,
\begin{align}
 f_q^{\circ q}(n)&=n+1-C_q(n),\label{eq:fC}\\
 a_q(n)&=2n+q+1-f_q^{\circ q}(n).\label{eq:hiccup-f}
\end{align}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The case $n=1$ is immediate. For $n\geq2$ write $n=L_k+r$ with
$k\geq1$ and $0\leq r\leq qk$, and put
$\ell=\min\{q,1+\left\lfloor r/k\right\rfloor\}$. On $[L_k,L_{k+1}-1]$ the map $f_q$
subtracts $k$, and on $[L_{k-1},L_k-1]$ it subtracts $k-1$, so
\[
 f_q^{\circ t}(L_k)=L_k-k-(t-1)(k-1)
 \qquad(1\leq t\leq q).
\]
These values lie in $[L_{k-1},L_k-1]$ and the last one is $L_{k-1}$
(for $k=1$ this interval is $\{1\}$, which $f_q$ fixes). As $f_q$ is
nondecreasing, the first $q$ iterates of $n$ do not fall below
$L_{k-1}$. The iterates $n,n-k,n-2k,\ldots$ remain in
$[L_k,L_{k+1})$ for $1+\left\lfloor r/k\right\rfloor$ steps, so exactly $\ell$ of the
first $q$ steps subtract $k$ and the others subtract $k-1$, which gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fblock}
 f_q^{\circ q}(n)=n-q(k-1)-\ell.
\end{equation}
By~\eqref{eq:cclosed},
\[
 c_q\bigl(q(k-1)+1+t\bigr)
 =1+q\binom{k}{2}+tk\qquad(0\leq t\leq q),
\]
and the next missing integer is $c_q(qk+2)=L_{k+1}$. The missing
integers up to $L_k+r$ are therefore those of index at most
$q(k-1)+1+\ell$, so $C_q(n)=q(k-1)+1+\ell$. This is~\eqref{eq:fC},
and~\eqref{eq:aC} gives~\eqref{eq:hiccup-f}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
For $q,n\geq1$,
\begin{equation}
 b_q^{\circ q}(n)=a_q(n)-1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Since $f_q(t)=1+\#\{k:b_q(k)<t\}$ (see~\cite[Section 6.1]{CloitreNested}),
we have, for positive integers $t$ and $n$,
\[
 f_q(t)\leq n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t\leq b_q(n).
\]
Applied $q$ times, the equivalence also holds for $f_q^{\circ q}$
and $b_q^{\circ q}$. By~\eqref{eq:fC},
$f_q^{\circ q}(t)=1+\#\{k:a_q(k)\leq t\}$, so $t\leq b_q^{\circ q}(n)$
if and only if $t<a_q(n)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
For $q\geq1$, $j\geq1$, and $t\geq0$, set
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal D_q(j,t)=c_q(j)+jt+q\binom{t+1}{2}.
\end{equation}
Every positive integer occurs exactly once in this array, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rowsuccessor}
 a_q(\mathcal D_q(j,t))=\mathcal D_q(j,t+1).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, order the pairs $(u,v)\in\mathbb N_0^2$ first by $u+qv$
and then by $v$. The rank of $(u,v)$, counted
from $1$, is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank}
 R_q(u,v)=c_q(u+1)+(u+1)v+q\binom{v+1}{2},
\end{equation}
and $a_q$ maps the rank of $(u,v)$ to the rank of $(u,v+1)$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Since $C_q(c_q(j))=j$, Theorem~\ref{thm:iterates} gives
$\mathcal D_q(j,t)=a_q^{\circ t}(c_q(j))$, which
proves~\eqref{eq:rowsuccessor}. Every value of $a_q$ has a unique
preimage, which is smaller. Starting from any positive integer and
repeatedly taking preimages therefore ends at a unique missing integer
$c_q(j)$ after a unique number $t$ of steps. Hence every positive
integer occurs exactly once in the array.

For the ranks, the number of pairs with $u+qv<h$ is
$\sum_{s=0}^{h-1}(\lfloor s/q\rfloor+1)=c_q(h+1)-1$, and among the
pairs of weight $u+qv$ exactly $v$ precede $(u,v)$. The rank of $(u,v)$
is therefore $c_q(u+qv+1)+v$, which becomes~\eqref{eq:rank} after $v$
applications of~\eqref{eq:comprec}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
Among polyominoes with $n\geq1$ cells, the least number of vertices,
that is, of lattice points that are corners of some cell, is
\begin{equation}
n+1+\left\lceil 2\sqrt n\right\rceil=a_2(n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $V$, $E$, $\mathcal P$, and $H$ be the numbers of vertices, unit
edges, boundary edges, and holes. Each cell has $4$ sides, and each
interior edge is shared by $2$ cells, so $E=2n+\mathcal P/2$.
Euler's formula $V-E+n=1-H$ gives
\[
V=n+1+\mathcal P/2-H.
\]
If the polyomino meets $h$ rows and $w$ columns, its outer boundary has
at least $2(h+w)$ edges and each hole boundary at least $4$, so
\[
V\geq n+1+h+w+H\geq n+1+\left\lceil 2\sqrt n\right\rceil+H,
\]
where the last step uses $n\leq hw$ and the integrality of $h+w$.

Equality holds for the polyominoes obtained from an $m\times m$ square
by adding cells one at a time along a new row until an $m\times(m+1)$
rectangle is reached, and then along a new column until an
$(m+1)\times(m+1)$ square is reached. They have no holes, and their
half-perimeter is $2m$ at $n=m^2$, $2m+1$ for $m^2<n\leq m(m+1)$, and
$2m+2$ for $m(m+1)<n\leq(m+1)^2$, which is $\left\lceil 2\sqrt n\right\rceil$ in each
case. Finally,
\[
n+1+\left\lceil 2\sqrt n\right\rceil=\left\lceil (1+\sqrt n)^2\right\rceil=a_2(n)
\]
by Proposition~\ref{prop:radical}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:monochromatic}
For $q,j,n\geq1$,
\begin{align}
 E_q(j+q-1)&=c_q(j)-1,\\
 a_q(n)-n&=\min\{N\geq0:E_q(N)\geq n\}.
\end{align}
Thus $a_q(n)-n$ is the least number of vertices for which every
coloring with $q$ colors has at least $n$ monochromatic pairs.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
If $v_i\geq v_{i'}+2$, moving a vertex from class $i$ to class $i'$
lowers the sum by $v_i-v_{i'}-1>0$, so the minimum is reached exactly
when all sizes differ by at most $1$. With $j-1=qm+r$ and $0\leq r<q$,
the balanced sizes for $N=j+q-1$ are $m+1$, taken $q-r$ times, and
$m+2$, taken $r$ times, hence
\[
 E_q(j+q-1)=(q-r)\binom{m+1}{2}+r\binom{m+2}{2}=c_q(j)-1.
\]
If $j=C_q(n)$, then $c_q(j)\leq n<c_q(j+1)$, that is,
$E_q(j+q-1)<n\leq E_q(j+q)$. Since $E_q$ is nondecreasing, the least
$N$ with $E_q(N)\geq n$ is $j+q$, which equals $a_q(n)-n$
by~\eqref{eq:aC}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
With the notation above,
\begin{align}
\operatorname{rc}(t_1,\ldots,t_\ell)
 &=D+1+C_1(p+1)\label{eq:multiramseyC}\\
 &=a_1(p+1)+D-p-1.
\end{align}
For two colors, this becomes
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{rc}(s,t)=a_1\bigl((s-1)(t-1)+1\bigr)-(s-2)(t-2).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $r=C_1(p+1)$. Since $c_1(j)=1+\binom j2$, we have
$\binom r2\leq p<\binom{r+1}2$, and as $p$ is an integer this gives
\[
r<\frac12+\sqrt{2p+\frac94}\leq r+1.
\]
Substituting in~\eqref{eq:bickle} yields the first identity,
and~\eqref{eq:aC} the second. For two colors, $D=s+t-2$ and
$p=(s-1)(t-1)$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
For $t\geq1$, let $r$ be the positive integer such that
$\binom r2<t\leq\binom{r+1}2$. Then
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{rc}(2,t)=t+r+1=a_1(t).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Write $t=\binom r2+s$ with $1\leq s\leq r$. A forest on $N$ vertices
has at most $N-1$ edges and a $(t-1)$-degenerate graph at most
$(t-1)N-\binom t2$, and for $N=t+r+1$
\[
\binom N2-(N-1)-\left((t-1)N-\binom t2\right)=r-s+1>0,
\]
so $\operatorname{rc}(2,t)\leq t+r+1$.

For the lower bound, take a rooted tree whose internal vertices form a
path $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ from the root, where $v_i$ has $r-i+1$ children,
including $v_{i+1}$ when $i<r$. This tree has $1+\binom{r+1}2$
vertices, and adding $s-1$ isolated vertices brings the total to
$t+r$. Color the tree edges red and all other edges of $K_{t+r}$ blue.
The red graph is a forest, and when $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ are deleted in
this order each has blue degree $t-1$, after which only $t$ vertices
remain, so the blue graph is $(t-1)$-degenerate. Since $r=C_1(t)$, we
get $t+r+1=a_1(t)$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
For integers $q\geq1$ and $D\geq q$, the maximum $\mathcal R_q(D)$
is attained when the $t_i$ differ by at most $1$, and
\begin{equation}
\mathcal R_q(D)
=D+1+C_1\!\left(\binom D2-c_q(D-q+1)+2\right).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
With $d_i=t_i-1$ and $D=\sum_id_i$ fixed,
\[
p=\sum_{i<j}d_id_j=\binom D2-\sum_i\binom{d_i}{2}
\]
is largest when the $d_i$ differ by at most $1$, and these balanced
values are positive because $D\geq q$. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:monochromatic},
\[
\max p=\binom D2-E_q(D)=\binom D2-c_q(D-q+1)+1,
\]
and the result follows from~\eqref{eq:multiramseyC}, since $C_1$ is
nondecreasing.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
